analysis.one_liner: Sets minimum safety, staffing, and resident-rights standards for board and care homes and raises benefits for their low-income residents.
analysis.headline: The bill died without a hearing or vote: introduced June 5, 1991 with no cosponsors, it was sent to two House committees and two subcommittees, and no further action was ever taken before the Congress ended on January 3, 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have created the first national minimum standards for board and care homes — small residential facilities that house elderly and disabled people who receive Social Security or disability benefits. It spelled out residents' rights, required trained administrators, staff on site at all times, safe buildings, proper medication handling, and unannounced state inspections at least every 15 months, with fines, temporary management, or closure for homes that put residents in danger. It also would have raised benefits for residents of certified homes by 10 percent, required states to top up very poor residents' income, and tightened tracking of payments made on behalf of people unable to manage their own money.
analysis.who_benefits: Elderly and disabled residents of board and care homes, most of whom live on Supplemental Security Income or disability benefits. They would gain enforceable rights (privacy, control over their own money and medications, freedom from abuse and restraints), regular unannounced inspections, a federal hotline for complaints, and a 10 percent benefit increase if they lived in a certified home. States would also benefit from federal reimbursement of 90 percent of inspection and enforcement costs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-income elderly and disabled care-home residents

how_it_helps.text: Establishes a detailed bill of rights for residents, including freedom from physical and chemical restraints, control over personal funds kept by the facility, and the right to see inspection results.

Requires every home to have a trained full-time administrator, staff present at all times, safe buildings, proper medication handling with monthly licensed-nurse visits, and meals meeting residents' dietary needs.

Requires states to conduct unannounced inspections at least every 15 months, investigate abuse complaints, hunt down unlicensed homes, and impose fines or temporary management or closure on dangerous facilities, with the federal government paying 90 percent of the cost.
Increases SSI benefits by 10 percent for residents of certified facilities and requires states to make supplementary payments to bring very poor residents up to the poverty line.

Requires monitoring of representative payees who manage benefits for people unable to handle their own money, including verifying the beneficiary is alive and in contact with the payee, to catch missing or misused payments.
Bars hospitals from discharging Medicare patients into homes that fail the standards and expands state Medicaid fraud units' work on care provided to residents.

analysis.who_pays: Board and care home operators, who would bear the cost of staffing, training, administrators, safety upgrades, and potential fines; and federal taxpayers, who would fund 90 percent of state inspection and enforcement costs, grants for training and emergency shelters, and the higher SSI benefit. States would carry new inspection and enforcement duties, mostly federally reimbursed.
analysis.who_pays_short: Care-home operators, states, and federal taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Staffing, administrator-training, and safety requirements would raise operating costs, and the bill's own design acknowledges the risk: it authorizes emergency shelters for residents displaced by endangered facilities and relocation aid paid for from fines.

Small and marginal homes serving very low-income residents could find compliance uneconomical and close, reducing the supply of inexpensive housing for people with few alternatives, and states would need to build inspection capacity even before the 90 percent federal reimbursement fully ramped up.

The bill relies on states to certify and enforce the standards, and federal validation inspections would cover only about 5 percent of facilities a year, so the quality of protection would depend heavily on state diligence.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections address a real, documented class of harm — elderly and disabled people in poorly supervised for-profit homes facing neglect, abuse, and theft of their benefit payments — and the bill pairs standards with 90 percent federal funding for enforcement and a direct benefit increase for residents. The main honest cost is that tougher standards could push some marginal operators out of the market and raise prices, which the bill partially anticipates with relocation and shelter funding. On balance the design is substantial and offsets much of the burden, though its heavy reliance on state enforcement is a real weakness.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees on the day it was introduced, farmed out to two subcommittees within two weeks, and then sat untouched until the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Edward Roybal introduced the National Board and Care Reform Act of 1991 on June 5, 1991.
The bill was referred the same day to both the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the House Ways and Means Committee, a joint referral that requires two committees to act.
It was referred to the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Human Resources on June 11 and the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health and the Environment on June 17.
No hearing, markup, or floor action ever followed; the last recorded action is the June 17, 1991 subcommittee referral, and the 102nd Congress ended January 3, 1993 with the bill still in committee.
The bill attracted no cosponsors at any point.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Operators of substandard or unlicensed board and care homes, who faced no new federal standards, inspections, or penalties, and state governments, which avoided new enforcement obligations. Residents of poor-quality homes gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Edward Roybal
for.role: Sponsor; chairman of the House Select Committee on Aging
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and handed it a detailed framework of standards, enforcement, and benefit increases for board and care residents.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee (Subcommittee on Human Resources)
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over SSI and Social Security titles of the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on June 5, 1991, sent it to its Human Resources Subcommittee on June 11, and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee (Subcommittee on Health and the Environment)
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the Medicare and Medicaid provisions
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on June 5, 1991, sent it to its Health and the Environment Subcommittee on June 17, and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the only recorded supporter was the Democratic sponsor and the bill drew no cosponsors from either party, so no partisan pattern can be measured from the record.

industries.note: Certified operators would take on real compliance costs but would become the permanent, federally-funded channel for housing SSI and disability beneficiaries, backed by a 10 percent richer payment stream, hospital discharge mandates, and public rewards for high quality. Substandard and unlicensed operators would face inspections, fines, and closure.
States would take on inspection, certification, and anti-fraud duties, but the federal government would reimburse 90 percent of the cost and pay for inspector training, making this a funded mandate.
Hospitals would face a new discharge-planning restriction barring them from sending Medicare patients to noncompliant homes and would have to report facility noncompliance to the state.
